source_text: Et haec quidem de patre et de filio et de spiritu sancto breuiter sint nobis dicta, et strictim posita, et non longa disputatione porrecta. latius enim potuerunt porrigi, et propensiore disputatione produci, quandoquidem ad testimonium, quod ita se habeat fides uera, totum et uetus et nouum testamentum possit adduci. sed quia obluctantes aduersus ueritatem semper haeretici sincerae traditionis et catholicae fidei controuersiam solent trahere, scandalizati in Christum, quod etiam deus et per scripturas asseratur et a nobis hoc esse credatur, merito a nobis (ut omnis a fide nostra auferri possit haeretica calumnia) de eo quod et deus sit Christus sic est disputandum, ut non impediat scripturae ueritatem, sed nec nostram fidem, qua unus deus et per scripturas promitur, et a nobis tenetur et creditur. tam enim illi qui Iesum Christum ipsum deum patrem dicunt, quam etiam illi qui hominem illum tantummodo esse uoluerunt, erroris sui et peruersitatis origines et causas inde rapuerunt, quia cum animaduerterent scriptum esse quod unus sit deus, non aliter putauerunt istam tenere se posse sententiam, nisi aut hominem tantum Christum, aut certe deum patrem putarent esse credendum. sic enim calumnias suas colligere consueuerunt, ut errorem proprium approbare nitantur. et quidem illi qui Iesum Christum patrem dicunt, ista praetendunt: si unus deus, Christus autem deus, pater est Christus, quia unus deus: si non pater sit Christus, dum et deus filius Christus, duo dii contra scripturas introducti esse uideantur. qui autem hominem tantummodo Christum esse contendunt, ex diuerso sic colligunt: si alter pater, alter est filius, pater autem deus, et Christus deus, non ergo unus deus, sed duo dii introducuntur pariter, pater et filius; ac si unus deus, consequenter homo Christus, ut merito pater sit deus unus. re uera quasi inter duos latrones cruci figitur dominus, quo modo fixus aliquando est: et ita excipit haereticorum istorum ex utroque latere sacrilega conuicia. Sed neque scripturae sanctae, neque nos causas illis perditionis et caecitatis afferimus, si qua in medio diuinarum ro litterarum euidenter posita aut uidere nolunt, aut uidere non possunt. nos enim et scimus et legimus et credimus et tenemus unum esse deum, qui fecit caelum pariter ac terram, quoniam nec alterum nouimus aut nosse (cum nullus sit) aliquando poterimus. ego sum, inquit, deus: e non est praeter me iustus et saluans. et alio in loco: ego primus et nouissimus, et praeter me non est deus. quis sicut ego? et: quis mensus est palmo caelum, et terram pugillo? quis suspendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera? et Ezechias: ut sciant omnes quia tu es deus solus. ipse praeterea dominus: quid me interrogas de bono? unus deus bonus. apostolus quoque Paulus: guz solus, inquit, habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem; quem uidit hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. et alio in loco: mediator autem unius non est; deus autem unus est. sed quo modo hoc tenemus et legimus et credimus, sic scripturarum caelestium nullam partem praeterire debemus: quippe cum etiam illa quae in scripturis sunt posita Christi diuinitatis insignia nullo modo debemus recusare, ne scripturarum auctoritatem corrumpendo integritatem fidei sanctae corrupisse teneamur. et hoc ergo credamus, siquidem fidelissimum, dei filium Iesum Christum dominum et deum nostrum: quoniam zz principio erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum. hoc erat in principio apud deum. et uerbum caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis. et: dominus meus et deus meus. et: quorum patres, et ex quibus Christus secundum carnem, qui est super omnia deus benedictus in saecula. Quid ergo dicemus? numquid duos deos scriptura proponit? quomodo ergo dicit, quia deus unus est? aut numquid non et Christus deus est? quomodo ergo, dominus meus et deus meus, Christo dictum est? totum igitur hoc nisi cum propria ueneratione et legitima disputatione teneamus, merito scandalum haereticis praebuisse credemur, non utique ex scripturarum caelestium uitio, quae numquam fallunt, sed humani erroris praesumptione, qua haeretici esse uoluerunt. et in primis illud retorquendum in istos qui duorum nobis deorum controuersiam facere praesumunt. scriptum est, quod negare non possunt, quoniam unus est dominus. de Christo ergo quid sentiunt? dominum esse, aut illum omnino non esse? sed dominum illum omnino non dubitant: ergo si uera est illorum ratiocinatio, iam duo sunt domini.. quomodo igitur iam secundum scripturas unus est dominus? et magister unus Christus est dictus; attamen legimus, quod magister sit etiam apostolus Paulus. non ergo iam unus magister: duos enim magistros secundum ista colligimus. quomodo igitur secundum scripturas unus magister Christus? unus in scripturis bonus dictus est deus; sed iisdem in scripturis bonus etiam Christus positus est. non igitur, si recte colligunt, unus bonus, sed etiam duo boni. quomodo igitur secundum scripturarum fidem unus bonus esse refertur? ac si non putant aliqua ratione offici posse ei quod unus dominus est, per illud quod est dominus et Christus; neque ei quod unus est magister, per illud quod est magister et Paulus; aut illi quod unus est bonus, per illud quod bonus sit nuncupatus et Christus; eadem ratione intellegant offici non posse ab illo quod unus est deus, ei quod deus pronuntiatus est et Christus.
pass_a_gloss: We have briefly stated these things about the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and have set them forth succinctly, and have not extended them in a long discussion. For they could have been extended more broadly, and produced with a more detailed discussion, since the whole of the Old and New Testament can be adduced as testimony that the true faith is such. But because heretics, who are always opposed to the truth, are accustomed to draw out a controversy against the sincere tradition and the Catholic faith, being scandalized by Christ, in that He is also God, as is asserted by the Scriptures and believed by us, it is right that we should discuss the fact that Christ is God in such a way that it does not hinder the truth of Scripture, nor our own faith, by which one God is promised and is held and believed by us through the Scriptures. For both those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father, and those who want Him to be only a man, have taken the origins and causes of their error from the fact that, when they noticed that it is written that there is one God, they did not think that they could hold this opinion in any other way, unless they thought that Christ was either only a man or certainly the Father. Thus, they are accustomed to collect their calumnies in such a way that they strive to approve their own error. And indeed, those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father, put forward this argument: if there is one God, and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; if Christ is not the Father, then, since He is the Son of God, two Gods are introduced, contrary to Scripture. But those who contend that Christ is only a man, collect their arguments in a contrary way: if the Father is one and the Son is another, and the Father is God, and Christ is God, then two Gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then consequently Christ is a man, so that the Father may be the one God. In truth, the Lord is crucified between two robbers, as He was once fixed to the cross, and thus He receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. But we do not bring forth the causes of their perdition and blindness, either from the Holy Scriptures or from ourselves, if they do not want to see, or cannot see, the things that are clearly set forth in the midst of the divine letters. For we know, and read, and believe, and hold that there is one God, who made heaven and earth, since we do not know, nor can we ever know, any other. 'I am,' He says, 'God, and there is no one just and saving besides Me.' And in another place: 'I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides Me.' 'Who is like Me?' And: 'Who has measured the heaven with a span, and the earth with a fist?' 'Who has suspended the mountains in a balance, and the woods in a scale?' And Ezechias: 'so that all may know that You are the only God.' The Lord Himself also says: 'Why do you ask Me about what is good? There is one good God.' The Apostle Paul also says: 'He alone has immortality, and He dwells in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see.' And in another place: 'A mediator of one is not; but God is one.' But just as we hold, and read, and believe this, so we ought not to pass over any part of the celestial Scriptures; for we ought not to refuse the signs of Christ's divinity that are set forth in the Scriptures, lest we be held to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures. And therefore, we believe, since it is most faithful, that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is our Lord and God; because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh, and dwelled among us. And: 'My Lord and my God.' And: 'whose fathers are, and from whom Christ is, according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever.' What then shall we say? Do the Scriptures propose two Gods? How then do they say that there is one God? Or do they not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ, 'My Lord and my God'? Therefore, unless we hold all this with proper veneration and legitimate discussion, we will be believed to have given scandal to the heretics, not because of any fault in the celestial Scriptures, which never fail, but because of the presumption of human error, by which the heretics have wanted to be. And first of all, we must retort to those who presume to make a controversy about two Gods, that it is written, which they cannot deny, that there is one Lord. What then do they think about Christ? That He is the Lord, or that He is not the Lord at all? But they do not doubt that He is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, then there are already two Lords. How then is it that, according to the Scriptures, there is one Lord? And it is said that there is one Master, Christ; yet we read that the Apostle Paul is also a master. Therefore, there is not one Master; for we gather from these things that there are two masters. How then, according to the Scriptures, is Christ one Master? One God is said to be good in the Scriptures; but in the same Scriptures, Christ is also said to be good. Therefore, if they reason correctly, there is not one good God, but two good Gods. How then, according to the faith of the Scriptures, is it said that there is one good God? And if they do not think that, by some reason of office, Christ can be the one Lord, because He is Lord, nor that He can be the one Master, because He is Master and Paul is master; nor that He can be the one good God, because He is called good and Christ is called good; by the same reason, they should understand that it is not possible to take away from the fact that there is one God, the fact that Christ is called God.

pass_b_english: We have stated these matters concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit briefly and succinctly, without drawing them out in a long discussion; they could have been treated more broadly and at greater length, since the whole of the Old and New Testament can be brought forward as testimony that the true faith is exactly this. But because heretics, always opposing the truth, habitually stir up controversy against the sincere tradition and the catholic faith, scandalized that Christ is also God — as Scripture asserts and as we believe — it is right that we should discuss the fact that Christ is God in such a way that we do not hinder the truth of Scripture, nor our own faith, by which one God is promised through the Scriptures and is held and believed by us. For both those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father and those who want him to be only a man have drawn the origins and causes of their error from the same source: when they noticed that it is written that there is one God, they did not think they could hold that opinion in any other way unless they thought Christ was either only a man or certainly the Father. In this manner they gather their calumnies so as to try to approve their own error. Those who say that Jesus Christ is the Father argue like this: if there is one God, and Christ is God, then Christ is the Father, because there is one God; if Christ is not the Father, then, since he is the Son of God, two gods are introduced contrary to Scripture. Those who contend that Christ is only a man argue in the opposite direction: if the Father is one and the Son is another, and the Father is God and Christ is God, then two gods are introduced, the Father and the Son; and if there is one God, then consequently Christ is a man, so that the Father may be the one God. In truth the Lord is crucified between two robbers, just as he was once fixed to the cross, and so he receives the sacrilegious insults of these heretics from both sides. Yet neither the Holy Scriptures nor we supply the causes of their perdition and blindness, if they either refuse to see or cannot see the things plainly set in the midst of the divine letters. For we know, read, believe, and hold that there is one God, who made heaven and earth alike, since we do not know any other, nor could we ever know one, because none exists. "I am," he says, "God, and there is no one just and saving besides me" (Isaiah 44:6). And elsewhere: "I am the first and the last, and there is no God besides me." "Who is like me?" And: "Who has measured the heavens with a span, and the earth with a fist? Who has suspended the mountains in a balance, and the woods in a scale?" And Hezekiah prayed: "that all may know that you are God alone." The Lord himself also says: "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is one good God." The apostle Paul also says: "He alone has immortality, and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see." And in another place: "A mediator of one is not; but God is one." But just as we hold, read, and believe this, so we ought not to pass over any part of the celestial Scriptures; for we must not refuse the signs of Christ's divinity that are set forth in the Scriptures, lest we be held to have corrupted the integrity of the holy faith by corrupting the authority of the Scriptures. Therefore let us believe — since it is most faithful — that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is our Lord and God; because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). He was in the beginning with God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). And Thomas said: "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). And: "whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever." What then shall we say? Do the Scriptures propose two gods? How then do they say that there is one God? Or do they not also say that Christ is God? How then was it said to Christ, "My Lord and my God"? Therefore, unless we hold all this with proper reverence and legitimate discussion, we shall be thought to have given scandal to the heretics — not because of any fault in the celestial Scriptures, which never fail, but because of the presumption of human error, by which the heretics chose to be heretics. And first of all we must retort to those who presume to make a controversy about two gods: it is written, which they cannot deny, that there is one Lord. What then do they think about Christ? That he is the Lord, or that he is not the Lord at all? But they do not doubt that he is the Lord; therefore, if their reasoning is true, there are already two Lords. How then, according to the Scriptures, is there one Lord? And it is said that there is one Master, Christ; yet we read that the apostle Paul is also a master. Therefore there is not one Master; for from these things we gather two masters. How then, according to the Scriptures, is Christ one Master? One God is called good in the Scriptures; but in the same Scriptures Christ is also called good. Therefore, if they reason correctly, there is not one good God, but two good Gods. How then, according to the faith of the Scriptures, is it said that there is one good God? And if they do not think that, by some reasoning of office, Christ can be the one Lord because he is Lord, nor that he can be the one Master because he is Master and Paul is master, nor that he can be the one good God because he is called good and Christ is called good; by the same reasoning they should understand that it is not possible to take away from the fact that there is one God the fact that Christ is called God.
